# SK3512 — A variable captured by `using` is returned

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`return x;` where `x` is owned by an enclosing `using`, so the caller receives an object that was disposed on the way out.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Lifetime |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| ReSharper | `ReturnOfUsingVariable` (`resharper_return_of_using_variable_highlighting`) |

## Why

A `using` disposes at the `return`, before the value reaches the caller, so the method's signature and its body disagree: it says "here is a resource" and delivers one that is already closed. The caller gets an `ObjectDisposedException` on first use, from a method that reads as correct — or, for a type whose `Dispose` only returns a pooled buffer, no exception at all and silent corruption once that buffer is handed to somebody else.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
Stream Open(string path) {
    using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);
    return stream;
}
```

Write:

```csharp
Stream Open(string path) => File.OpenRead(path);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **No fix, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** Deleting the `using` makes the method leak; keeping it makes the method wrong. Which the author meant is the whole question and no edit answers it, so the finding is a report. ⚠ **The `Task` shape belongs to `SK3007`.** The two rules overlap on exactly one shape — `return x;` where `x` is a `using` variable of a task type — and `SK3007` is the one carrying a fix for it, so this rule tests the type and stays quiet rather than being deduplicated after the fact. `supersedes` was considered and rejected: it dedupes on a shared span and would have suppressed the finding that has the fix. Where `SK3007` declines the shape because it cannot rewrite the whole method, neither rule reports, which is a known gap. ⚠ **The returned expression must be the variable itself.** `return x.Stream;` and `return Wrap(x);` hand out something whose lifetime may well depend on `x`, and proving that needs to know what the member or the method did with it; guessing about ownership is how a rule comes to report the correct code around the incorrect code. ⚠ The `return` and the `using` must belong to the same member, lambda or local function: a `return` inside a lambda returns from the lambda, and a lambda closing over a `using` variable may run at a time the `using` says nothing about.
